In brief

Parody. "He said and then lifted he in his rude great brawny strengthy hands [...] sit on thrones of alabaster silent as the deathless gods": continuing the vein of faux medieval heroism, this sentence makes the Citizen into a mighty Celtic warrior urging his followers to battle. It saves its funniest barb, however, for the Englishmen whom he is verbally assailing.

At more length

The first words of the sentence, "He said," suggest that it will refer to Lenehan, who has just delivered one of his clever little mots. But the grammatical subject is surely the Citizen, who for quite a few paragraphs now has been loudly attacking the English, their language, and their "syphilisation." The following words make that inference inescapable: "and then lifted he in his rude great brawny strengthy hands the medher of dark strong foamy ale." The language here reprises the earlier parodic description of the Citizen as a "sinewyarmed hero" like to the great Cuchulain. Here, "uttering his tribal slogan Lamh Dearg Abu, he drank to the undoing of his foes." Lámh Dearg Abú, Red Hand to Victory, was the battle cry of the powerful O'Neill clan in Ulster. Slote, Mamigonian, and Turner helpfully quote the OED's definition of "slogan" as "A war-cry or battle cry; spec. one of those formerly employed by Scottish Highlanders or Borderers, or by the native Irish, usually consisting of a personal surname or the name of a gathering place."

The parody furthers its aim of converting the Citizen into a lusty medieval warrior by putting his porter into a "medher," a ceremonial Celtic drinking vessel. The medher (or mether, or meadar), whose name is thought to derive from Mehill = gathering, was used for drinking mead. Originally carved from single blocks of wood (later ones were made of ceramic or metal), these large communal cups had either two or four handles, making it easy to pass them along a banqueting table as warriors celebrated their victories. The Gaelic Athletic Association, an organization that the Citizen's model Michael Cusack founded, has kept the tradition alive to the present day, presenting methers as celebratory trophy cups for some sports championships. 

As for the man's "foes," they too get the heroic treatment at first, being called "a race of mighty valorous heroes, rulers of the waves." But Joyce cannot rest content with repeating the Brits' boast about their navy. Picking up on the Citizen's statement just before the parody that "You wouldn't see a trace of them or their language anywhere in Europe except in a cabinet d'aisance" (the French word for a watercloset), he returns to the scornful chauvinism of Aeolus, where Professor MacHugh proclaimed that the ancient Roman, like the modern Englishman, had a "cloacal obsession. He gazed about him in his toga and he said: It is meet to be here. Let us construct a watercloset." The parody's picture of British warriors who "sit on thrones of alabaster silent as the deathless gods" is hilarious. The throne they revere is a toilet, but they're too repressed to say much about it.


John Hunt 2026
